 APEX PREDATORS
 Influencer Indicted for Hunting White Shark off Wellfleet
 Christopher Stefanou to have December pretrial hearing on animal cruelty charges
 By Jack Styler Oct 28, 2026 
 WELLFLEET — A fishing “trip of a lifetime” to Wellfleet has come back to bite a Long Island man.
 A screenshot from the video Christopher Stefanou posted online about his October 2025 shark hunt in Wellfleet shows a large shark on the shore. (Photo by Christopher Stefanou) 
 Christopher Stefanou, 30, was arraigned on Oct. 21 after a Barnstable County grand jury returned indictments against him on charges of cruelty to animals and four Dept. of Marine Fisheries (DMF) regulatory violations for fishing for a great white shark off Marconi Beach under cover of darkness with a European customer a year ago.
 Stefanou, who has a sizable online following for his shark fishing, posted a dramatic 17-minute video on social media documenting the expedition. The video ends with Stefanou, his crew, and a man referred to only as “Matt” from Amsterdam landing a white shark on the beach.
 The shark was one that’s known to scientists who are studying how their presence helps preserve a balanced marine ecosystem. It had been tracked by the Atlantic White Shark Conservancy since it was first tagged on Aug. 27, 2024, and prosecutors at the arraignment estimated the shark’s weight at around 1,000 pounds.
 Great white sharks are a federally protected species; it is illegal to fish for them. The DMF violations are for shore-based shark fishing, possessing a prohibited species, mechanical deployment of bait, and attracting and capturing a white shark.
 Prosecutors at first made the case that the shark, which researchers had named AAron, was believed to have died from capture stress from the incident, but the shark was later pinged (its tag detected by a location sensor) far from Wellfleet, prosecutor Emily Nesson Cardia said at Stefanou’s bail hearing.
 An increase in large-shark fishing in the waters around Cape Cod, and an incident in September 2024 in which surfers at LeCount Hollow Beach called Wellfleet police after a group of fishermen used drone-assisted baited lines to lure sharks, have motivated state officials to tighten regulations.
 In March of last year, the Mass. Marine Fisheries Advisory Commission voted to ban the use of drones to drop bait and wire leaders longer than 18 inches, the Independent has reported. 
 Dr. Greg Skomal, a marine biologist and shark expert with the DMF, helped prosecutors with the investigation, according to a press release from District Attorney Rob Galibois’s office.
 Skomal did not respond to questions about the case, but Julia Hopkins, a spokesperson for the DMF, said that in recent years the DMF has heard more accounts of shark fishing on the outer beaches of Cape Cod and on Nantucket and descriptions of anglers using heavy rod and reel gear and mechanized bait deployment to target white sharks.
 Regulations have historically prohibited targeting or attempting to attract great white sharks, which are present in the greatest numbers off Cape Cod in September and October, both because the practice poses a serious public safety risk and can harm the apex predators, said Hopkins.
 This appears to be the first time someone has been prosecuted for fishing for great white sharks in the U.S.
 Stefanou pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him. After the arraignment, he declined to comment, said his lawyer, Jon Ciraulo.
 “The charges against Chris are allegations only,” said Ciraulo. “He maintains his innocence and intends to fully challenge the allegations.”
 Ciraulo said Stefanou “is a skilled and accomplished angler with more than a decade of experience” and noted that he “actively participates” in conservation practices, marine tagging, and volunteers his time educating “enthusiasts on safe and responsible angling.”
 According to a New York Times report that featured Stefanou, his version of shark tagging is problematic. “One of the misconceptions is that they’re helping science, because they’re collecting data and tagging the sharks,” Greg Metzger, field coordinator for the shark research program at the South Fork Natural History Museum on Long Island, told the Times. “The problem is the handling of the shark,” he said, “and that’s where the real issue is.”
 A ‘Sharkman’ and Video Star 
 Boasting about 2.2 million subscribers on YouTube and hundreds of thousands of followers on other social media platforms, Stefanou has found success and notoriety by chronicling his conquests online, posting under the name “Lisharkman.”
 Stefanou recently filmed a shark-fishing expedition with the current number one Ultimate Fighting Championship pound-for-pound fighter, Islam Makhachev, posting the video afterward. The Independent has viewed the video, although it has since been removed from Stefanou’s social media page.
 Stefanou’s practice of posting his fishing exploits online now seems to have provided a foundation for the prosecutor’s animal cruelty charge, which carries a maximum sentence of seven years in prison.
 A video of the events of the current case, which Stefanou called “The Largest Great White Shark Ever Caught From Shore on Film,” starts in New York City’s LaGuardia Airport, where Stefanou is waiting to pick up “Matt,” a longtime customer of his who flies in from Amsterdam.
 The men never say where they’re going. The instantly recognizable skyline of New York City fades into a short clip that looks like Route 6. In a rented house, which prosecutors alleged is in Orleans, Stefanou, Matt, and the rest of the crew briefly discuss weather conditions for fishing.
 In the next scene, it’s dark and they’re on a beach. What the men call “Operation Amsterdam” begins.
 Stefanou uses drones baited with bluefish and cobia heads to drop lines far offshore. The lines are connected to their rods, which are secured in the sand.
 Eventually, they get a bite.
 Stefanou hands the rod to Matt, who despite being rigged with a fishing harness to secure the rod, needs others to hold him to keep him from being pulled into the ocean by the white shark on the other end of the line.
 After a prolonged battle that prosecutors allege went on for more than an hour, the nine-and-a-half-foot shark, exhausted, nears shore.
 “Oh my,” the man behind the camera is heard saying, as the giant bloodied shark comes into focus with large waves tumbling over it.
 While the shark is briefly beached, the men gather around it to take a photo. Stefanou uses a tool that removes the hook from the shark’s mouth and releases the animal back into the ocean.
 “AAron the Shark” disappears into the darkness. Matt crumples to his knees, seemingly overcome with emotion.
 As the video closes, Matt thanks Stefanou and his crew for a “trip of a lifetime.”
 “AAron the Shark” had been pinged 5,030 times since he was first tagged in 2024, according to the Atlantic White Shark Conservancy’s logbook app. After Stefanou allegedly caught the shark on Oct. 22, 2025, it appeared to move south toward Chatham, based on his receiver pings. The shark was last pinged that November.
 Following the grand jury’s indictment, as a part of the judge’s bail conditions, Stefanou was required to take down all content related to the alleged white shark fishing incident, including the video.
 Judge Elaine Buckley ordered him not to fish in Massachusetts waters, promote his company, or post about the incident. Stefanou was released on $10,000 bail and is scheduled to appear in Barnstable Superior Court again on Dec. 11 for a pretrial hearing.
